title: Bash
summary: Drive a computer from the command line: navigate, combine commands with pipes, and write scripts.

lessons.title: Bash: navigating and managing files

concept.text:
Bash is a **shell**: a program that reads commands you type and runs them. It is the default way to control Linux servers, cloud machines and most developer tools.

A command is a program name followed by options (starting with `-`) and arguments. `ls -a logs` means: run `ls`, with the option `a`, on the folder `logs`.
concept.analogy: A graphical desktop is ordering by pointing at pictures on a menu. The shell is speaking the language: harder at first, but you can ask for exactly what you want, and ask for it a thousand times in a row.

visual.caption: Ten commands that cover most daily work.

items.title: pwd
items.text: Print the folder you are in

items.title: rm file
items.text: Delete. There is no recycle bin!

steps.title: Find out where you are
steps.text: Every shell has a current folder. Paths that do not start with `/` are relative to it.

steps.title: Move around
steps.text: `cd logs` goes down into logs. `cd ..` goes up. `cd` alone goes home.

steps.title: Create and inspect
steps.text: Make a folder, create a file in it, and read a file.
steps.code:
mkdir projects
touch projects/todo.txt
cat notes.txt

steps.title: Copy, rename, delete
steps.text: Be careful with `rm`: deleted files are gone for good.
steps.code:
cp notes.txt backup.txt
mv backup.txt old-notes.txt
rm old-notes.txt

interactive.starter:
pwd
ls

cat notes.txt

mkdir projects
touch projects/todo.txt
cp notes.txt projects/notes-copy.txt
ls projects

cd logs
pwd
ls

challenge.prompt: Create a folder called `archive`, move `notes.txt` into it renamed as `notes-2024.txt`, then list the `archive` folder to prove it worked.
challenge.hint: `mv` both moves and renames: `mv source destination/newname`.
challenge.solution:
mkdir archive
mv notes.txt archive/notes-2024.txt
ls archive

takeaways: A command is a program name, options and arguments.
pwd, ls and cd let you navigate. mkdir, touch, cp, mv and rm manage files.
rm is permanent. Check with ls before you delete.

lessons.title: Bash: pipes, redirects, variables and loops

concept.text:
The shell's superpower is combining small tools. A **pipe** (`|`) sends one command's output into the next command's input. A **redirect** (`>`) sends output into a file instead of the screen.

Add variables and loops, and a few lines can process thousands of files.
concept.analogy: Each command is a single Lego brick that does one thing. The pipe is the stud that snaps bricks together into a machine.

visual.caption: A pipeline: each command transforms the stream of text.

steps.title: Search with grep
steps.text: `grep` prints the lines that match a pattern. `-c` counts them and `-i` ignores case.
steps.code:
grep ERROR logs/app.log
grep -c INFO logs/app.log

steps.title: Pipe commands together
steps.text: Count the lines in a file by piping `cat` into `wc -l`.

steps.title: Redirect to a file
steps.text: `>` overwrites the file and `>>` appends to it.
steps.code:
echo "first line" > out.txt
echo "second line" >> out.txt

steps.title: Variables and loops
steps.text: No spaces around `=`. Read a variable with `$`. `$(...)` captures a command's output.
steps.code:
NAME="world"
echo "Hello, $NAME"
for f in notes.txt logs/app.log; do
  echo "$f has $(cat $f | wc -l) lines"
done

interactive.starter:
grep ERROR logs/app.log

cat logs/app.log | grep INFO | wc -l

grep ERROR logs/app.log | sort > errors.txt
cat errors.txt

NAME="learner"
echo "Hello, $NAME. You are in $(pwd)"

for f in notes.txt logs/app.log; do
  echo "$f has $(cat $f | wc -l) lines"
done

challenge.prompt: Write one pipeline that prints the **last** line of `notes.txt` when its lines are sorted alphabetically.

takeaways: A pipe | feeds one command's output to the next.
> writes output to a file and >> appends.
Variables, $(...) and for loops turn commands into automation.

lessons.title: Bash mini project: a log report script

concept.text: System administrators live in log files. You will write a script that summarises a log: how many lines, how many errors, and a warning if errors pass a threshold. Scripts like this get scheduled to run every few minutes on real servers.
concept.analogy: The script is a night watchman with a checklist. It walks the same route every time, counts what it sees, and only wakes you if something is wrong.

steps.title: Start with a shebang
steps.text: The first line of a real script tells the system which shell runs it. Make the file executable with `chmod +x report.sh`, then run `./report.sh`.

steps.title: Test a condition
steps.text: `[ a -gt b ]` is true when a is greater than b. The spaces inside the brackets are required.
steps.code:
if [ $ERRORS -gt 1 ]; then
  echo "ALERT"
else
  echo "OK"
fi

interactive.starter:
LOG=logs/app.log
LIMIT=1

TOTAL=$(cat $LOG | wc -l)
ERRORS=$(grep -c ERROR $LOG)

echo "Log: $LOG"
echo "Lines: $TOTAL"
echo "Errors: $ERRORS"

grep ERROR $LOG > report.txt
echo "--- report.txt ---"
cat report.txt

if [ $ERRORS -gt $LIMIT ]; then
  echo "ALERT: more than $LIMIT error(s)"
else
  echo "All good"
fi

challenge.prompt: Extend the script to also print the percentage of lines that are errors, for example `Error rate: 40%`.
challenge.hint: Bash arithmetic uses `$(( ))`. Multiply before dividing because Bash only does whole numbers: `$((ERRORS * 100 / TOTAL))`.

takeaways: A script is a file of commands, starting with #!/bin/bash.
$(command) captures output and $((math)) does integer arithmetic.
if [ ... ] tests conditions: -gt, -lt and -eq compare numbers.
